I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

I should have protected others and I failed

vignette: Arthur Vance sat in his quiet living room, but his mind had drifted back to the concrete cell where the torture began. He was never given a clear timeline, only a series of violent intrusions that left him stranded between moments of blinding clarity and long, suffocating blanks. Some flashes remained seared into his mind, but the rest of what happened simply vanished. When those fragments returned, the terror he felt at the time rushed back with them, unsoftened by time. Because he viewed his own helplessness through such a harsh lens, this memory of the gaps only deepened his shame; every time the distress surfaced, his mind filled the blanks with accusations, convincing him that he was a weak person and that he should have protected the others, but he failed. The trauma’s geometry now dictated his daily routine. Working the night routes as a bus driver had become an exercise in constant appraisal. As the recalled terror of confinement grew more vivid, it directly triggered his physical reactivity; the moment the bus brakes squealed or the suspension hit a pothole, his chest would constrict and his breath would shallow, a physiological alarm that felt identical to the past. His persistent belief that he was a weak person and that he failed to protect others directly fueled his threat system; every minor creak in the night became evidence that he was still too powerless to keep himself safe. He began taking the longest, most illuminated routes home, spending the last ten minutes parked in his driveway with the engine off, listening intently for sounds that might mean someone was entering his home. He found it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, and the constant scanning left him exhausted. As the weeks bled into months, his memories and appraisals locked into a relentless pattern. The incomplete picture of the event did not just haunt him; it actively shaped his negative self-view. Every time he recalled the terror, the missing pieces of the timeline felt like evidence of his own inadequacy, pushing him to believe he ought to have known how to stop it. Conversely, his lingering guilt and sense of weakness constantly pulled him back into those memories, magnifying the distress and making the fragments feel more immediate. His physical reactivity in the driver’s seat became impossible to ignore; the moment the bus brakes squealed or a passenger spoke too loudly, his chest would constrict and his breath would shallow, a physiological alarm that convinced him the danger was still active. This heightened threat monitoring only made his negative appraisals more rigid, as his own nervous system’s responses were interpreted as proof of his failure. The consequences mounted quietly but firmly: he declined the overnight shift, citing health reasons, and began avoiding the bus depot's loading bay, where the echoing acoustics reminded him of the cell. His marriage grew strained, not from anger, but from the exhaustion of a man who felt perpetually on the brink of collapse. He finally came to therapy because the avoidance was no longer holding the fear at bay. He was terrified that the physical reactivity would escalate into a panic attack on the road, that his inability to feel safe at night would eventually unravel his marriage, and that he was trapped in a loop he could not break. He hoped someone could help him untangle the memories without forcing him to confront the guilt, hoping to reclaim a sense of strength that had been stripped away long ago.
